Q: NASM - error: label or instruction expected at start of line A:

After working with iuppiter it was determined that Visual Studio was writing the assembler file with wrong file encoding. The side effect was that NASM was unable to parse the file and exited with:

boot.asm:1: error: label or instruction expected at start of line

To resolve this problem in Visual Studio 2015 one can save the file with a different encoding using this process:

  1. Open the assembler file
  2. Select File/Save as... on the menu
  3. At the bottom of the file selector window click the down arrow beside the Save button at the bottom
  4. Click Save with encoding...
  5. Select Western European (Windows) Codepage 1252 (This should be plain text)
  6. Click OK

Q: Controller hotplugging issue A:

I think you need to initialise the controllers and track them using a dictionary or a list.

Without joystick.init() the controllers are not being activated and ready to use. This is separate from the pygame.init(), it has it's own life cycle.

Try this example:

import pygame

pygame.joystick.init()
joysticks = [pygame.joystick.Joystick(x) for x in range(pygame.joystick.get_count())]

print(joysticks)

So in your case you want to listen to the adding event:

joysticks = {}
if event.type == pygame.JOYDEVICEADDED:
    joystick = pygame.joystick.Joystick(event.device_index) 
    joystick.init()

    joysticks[joystick.get_instance_id()] = joystick

    print("Added:", joystick.get_name())

Make sure you remove the controller from the list when it's disconnected:

elif event.type == pygame.JOYDEVICEREMOVED:
    joysticks.pop(event.instance_id, None)
    print("Removed:", event.instance_id)

However in your case i see the device index are both 0 so I am not sure what will happen; but you can use get_count as in the example above and track them yourself, or maybe you can use the GUID. Its up to you, use what works in your case.

Q: Compiling C/GTK within Eclipse A:

A way to Compile and Link GTK in Eclipse

My Setup
    Debian Linux
    Eclipse Version 2026-06 (4.40.0) IDE for C/C++ Developers

Prerequisites
    Have installed gtk4 via pkg-config.
    Successfully compiled and linked a gtk4 hello world program via the terminal command line.

1) Create: File -> New -> C/C++ Project -> Classic C Project -> Next
2) Give the project a name.
3) If not already checked, check "Use default location"
4) For "Project type" choose "Hello World ANSI C Project"
5) For "Toolchains" select "Linux GCC". 
6) Click "Finish"
7) In "Project Explorer" expand the folder with your project name
8) Copy the GTK "Hello World" C file, possibly from 
    https://www.gtk.org/docs/getting-started/hello-world
9) Expand src and double click the "project name.c" file to open it
10) Select all of the .c file source code and paste over it with GTK "Hello World" code
11) Save the .c file
12) Click "Project" dropdown, click "Properties", expand "C/C++ Build, click "Settings"
13) Click "GCC C Compiler". 
"Expert settings: Command line pattern:" reads:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}
Edit this to read:
${COMMAND} $(shell pkg-config --cflags gtk4) ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}

14) Click "GCC C Linker"
"Expert settings: Command line pattern:" reads:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS}
Edit this to read:
${COMMAND} ${FLAGS} ${OUTPUT_FLAG} ${OUTPUT_PREFIX}${OUTPUT} ${INPUTS} ${EXTRA_FLAGS} ${shell pkg-config --libs gtk4}
Notes:
Keep the white spacing as it is. The spacing carries through to the GCC command.
Also keep the order of the $(...) commands. The compiler flags ("cflags") are placed following the GCC command because when compilation is successfully completed, linking is performed (I believe eclipse calls the ld command). If the libraries ("libs") are placed earlier in the order, they'll go to the compiler instead of the linker. 

"shell" in the added command causes expansion of the package before it is sent to the compiler or linker.

The ${...} syntax is the modern form of the old `...` backtick syntax. They are very similar in effect. 

Learn a bit more (optional): Run "pkg-config --cflags gtk4" and "pkg-config --libs gtk4" from your Linux terminal command line.

Q: Bag of Words without images A:

"Bag of Words" as a term is inaccurate. OpenCV, not being a NLP library but a Computer Vision library, offers you code that deals with "bags of visual words". The "matchers" it offers are for "local feature descriptors", which describe small patches of image content.

"visual words" has actually nothing to do with words. It does have to do with clustering.

Since you want text, not images, you picked the wrong library. To put it differently, you are barking up the wrong tree.

Q: How can I get this Apple-like image sequence animation to start in the middle of the website, instead of only on top? A:

The trick is to take the "animation sequence" offsetTop into account and use its scrollHeight to calculate the maxScrollTop:

const scrollTop = document.documentElement.scrollTop - heroSequence.offsetTop
const maxScrollTop = heroSequence.scrollHeight - window.innerHeight

The apple-sequence-animation project is on my Github.
